To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
H. pylori undergoes coccoid transition and decreases in proliferation and urease activity after exposure to oxidative stress.
oxidative‐stress conditions can induce a dramatic decrease in the protein expression levels and activities of UreE and alkylhydroproeroxide reductase in H. pylori.

H. pylori cells incubated under oxidative stress displayed decreased proliferation, loss of urease and antioxidant ability, which are accompanied by the decreased protein expressions of UreE and AlhpC, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the proteomic analysis of proteins of Helicobacter, which are differentially expressed under aerobic and microaerophil conditions.
a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying H. pylori adaptation and survival in the host environment.
the identification of the proteins that are differentially expressed in H. pylori in response to oxidative stress, which is a major challenge for the bacterium in the host environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

oxidative stress can lead to a decrease of urease and AhpC expression in H. pylori, and the decrease of urease activity in turn may be responsible for the coccoid morphology of H. pylorii under aerobic stress.

the loss of urea activity and the decrease of anti‐oxidative capability are due to the down‐regulation of urease accessory proteins (UreE and UreF) and antioxidant proteins (AhpC and AhpF) under oxidative stress, respectively.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oxidative stress induces a cascade of cellular responses, including morphological change, loss of urease and antioxidant activities, and down‐regulation of gene expression.
H. pylori can be considered as a facultative anaerobe, and oxidative stress is a major threat to its survival in vivo.
oxidative stress induces morphological changes, inhibits proliferation, and down‐regulates the expression of urease and anti‐oxidant proteins in H. pylori.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oxidative stress is a potent factor in modulating protein expression of H. pyloris, and that this may have a significant impact on its virulence and pathogenicity.

the oxidative stress‐induced changes in protein expression profiles can be used as an effective tool for the discovery of new therapeutic targets for the development and design of novel anti‐H. pylori agents.
H. pylori is a versatile bacterium that can adapt to different environmental conditions by regulating its gene expression profile and protein synthesis.
